newsitem.title: INDIA: India sugar export decontrol could backfire - industry.
newsitem.headline: India sugar export decontrol could backfire - industry.

text.p: India's proposal to end a trading agency's monopoly over sugar exports could backfire on an industry whose costs are higher than international prices, traders and officials said on Monday.
"Our cost of production is higher because of partial decontrol," said Yatin Wadhwana, executive director of Bhopal Sugar Industries Ltd.
"If they totally decontrol, then our cost of production will be the same or even lower than international prices," he said.
Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda said on Sunday he planned to issue a decree, bypassing parliament, to allow registered private entrepreneurs to export sugar.

Last week, India's lower house of parliament approved a bill taking the sole right to export away from the Indian Sugar and General Industries Export-Import Corp (ISGIEC), an agency set up by private millers.
But the upper house stalled the bill, telling the government that the issue needed further study.
The move could lead to competing mills undercutting on export prices, and export sales drying up as traders are exposed to mounting losses, an ISGIEC official said.
Traders said the government must produce a clearer policy on how it plans to implement the decision.
Industry officials said under the current regime, losses incurred by ISGIEC on exports were borne by sugar factories on the basis of allotments made to them for exports.
They said the cost of producing sugar in India was higher than the export prices because of government controls.
Sugar supplies and pricing in India are controlled by the government.
The mills supply 40 percent of the output as a levy at a subsidised rate for distribution among the poor and sell the balance in the open market, regulated over a period of 12 months.
Industry officials said that the average cost of production of sugar in India was about 11,500-12,000 rupees per tonne and it was supplied to the government at 8,800 rupees per tonne.
The need to cut stocks and generate foreign currency were driving export sales despite low world prices, an official of the National Federation of Cooperative Sugar Factories said.
"As far as (the) sugar industry is concerned, we are exporting to cut bulging stocks and earn precious foreign exchange," he said. "But international prices now are low."
Deve Gowda said on Sunday there were some 3.5 million tonnes of sugar stored in depots around the country that India wanted to sell, and his decree could help this sugar reach the market.
Food Minister Devendra Prasad Yadav told parliament on Thursday that the new measure would ensure production of good quality sugar and allow mills to export directly.

India began abolishing licenses for many industries under a reform programme that began in 1991, but it kept sugar under the old regime, which has subsidised prices for consumers and protected producers.
